We are goats🐐. 

We are high school students at Liberty High School, Frisco who are interested in Aerospace Engineering🐐. We have won awards in multiple NASA related competitions like Space Teams and Space Apps 2025 and A&M competitions like Aggies Invent Jr 🐐.
summary: We developed a single-player 2D Martian Base Simulator to allow young learners to learn about the resources to maintain at a base and the challenges astronauts have to overcome while exploring extraterrestrial bodies. Our simulation is interactive and fun to play, making it an enjoyable resource to learn about the split-second decisions astronauts have to make in space without making it overly challenging to deter youths from playing the game. Our project contains all the necessary obstacles and resources an actual NASA mission might have, giving the players a realistic experience of managing a base on Mars. It is important as the next generation is the one that will lead crewed missions to planets and other celestial bodies to explore for potential places where human life could survive. Since the youths of today are going to be those explorers, they should build experience and understanding of the workings of a habitat on another planet in order to maximize our knowledge on the vast expanse of the universe.

TO PLAY THE GAME:

CLICK ON THE LINK ON THE TOP OF THE README FILE IN THE GITHUB REPOSITORY LINKED BELOW OR CLICK HERE - https://ssurpluss.itch.io/red-domain

What it does and how it works
Red Domain is a 2D top-down survival and base-building simulator. The player is a super-goat, the first and only goat sent to Mars, guided by an onboard AI called Mechaguru through a retro space-themed dialogue system.

Players first choose cargo under a strict 40-ton limit. Required items include metal walls, an airlock door, solar panels, batteries, water, grass, an air purifier, a command console, and Super Goat-Glue 4000. Optional gear includes a Mars Rover, a Radiation Shield, and a Food Tastifier (which visibly boosts the hunger value of every meal by 60%). Players construct an air-tight base inside a surveyor grid—keeping solar panels outdoors—and activate the command console to begin the survival phase.

No rescue is coming: players must survive 30 Martian minutes while managing health, oxygen, power, hunger, thirst, and radiation. Red dust storms sweep across the screen and break solar panels, marsquakes fracture the terrain and breach walls, and being caught outside during a disaster drains health rapidly. Players patch broken structures with Super Goat-Glue 4000 through an interactive wiring mini-game, equip their radiation shield or drive the rover across the desert to salvage rare unannounced meteorite crashes for rations, cryo-ice, and oxygen canisters, and learn from detailed fail screens that explain the exact cause of death and how to solve it on the next run.

Benefits
The game teaches real mission-planning tradeoffs: every ton launched to Mars matters, life support must be budgeted, and power systems require backups. Failure is built into the learning loop, because each fail screen diagnoses what went wrong and gives an actionable fix. Simple controls and lighthearted humor keep younger players engaged, and the lightweight build runs smoothly on ordinary school and home laptops.

Intended impact
We want space exploration to feel like a hands-on puzzle anyone can solve. Every hazard is grounded in real Martian science—global dust storms, marsquakes detected by NASA’s InSight lander, surface radiation exposure, and oxygen generation inspired by Perseverance’s MOXIE experiment. After one playthrough, players understand why astronauts train and why off-world missions require careful engineering.

Tools and technology
We built Red Domain in Unity 6.6 (Personal plan) with C#, using the Universal 2D template and the Unity Input System package. All pixel art sprites and sound effects are generated procedurally in C# code, paired with an open-licensed pixel font. We developed on Windows laptops and used AI assistance to help write and iterate on the C# scripts while we directed the game design, art direction, and playtesting.

Creativity
Serious planetary science meets absurd lore: an astronaut goat stranded on Mars with Mechaguru. The 40-ton mass budget forces real engineering decisions, while joke items like a golden throne or disco ball tempt players to waste payload capacity. Instead of fictional monsters, escalating Martian weather, terrain fractures, and unannounced meteorite impacts drive the tension.

Factors we considered

Scope: Built in focused milestones with procedural art and audio so the game stayed playable from start to finish.

Balance: A bare-minimum kit is viable with smart scavenging, while optional gear like the Rover, Radiation Shield, and Food Tastifier reward careful cargo planning.

Audience: Non-violent, intuitive controls, large readable UI, and clear diagnostic tips after every failure.

Accuracy vs. fun: Real Martian hazards translated into clear visual cues, mini-games, and fast-paced survival decisions.

Accessibility: Ultra-lightweight footprint with zero large external asset downloads.
